In the 1980s, Alan, Wayne, Merrill and Jay regrouped as a country act, releasing "One Way Rider." Their hits included "I Think About Your Lovin.'" At the time, Alan told The Associated Press he switched from recording rock to country music because it better fit their wholesome image. "Country music really is the backbone of America," he said. "It doesn't just come and go. And we're kind of flag-wavers. You find that in the country area, too." He also helped lead Stadium of Fire, an annual July Fourth celebration in Provo, Utah, that is one of the largest in the country. Four of Alan's own children formed another group, The Osmond Boys, also known as The Osmonds Second Generation. In 1987, Alan was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, and in the late '90s retreated from touring. He helped create the Children's Miracle Network, which aids children's hospitals, and with his wife Suzanne founded the humanitarian organization OneHeart. Doug Osmond, one of Alan's sons, told The AP of his dad: "I've never met anyone more positive in my life. I never once heard him complain, not once. He would say, 'I may have MS, but MS does not have me.' That was his motto and he always was worried about everyone else. ... Family always took priority and his faith was in everything he did."

Desmond Morris Desmond Morris with the chimpanzee Congo on the TV program "Zoo Time," 1956. | Desmond Morris Collection/Universal Images Group via Getty Images As a young boy, English zoologist Desmond Morris (Jan. 24, 1928-April 19, 2026) watched his father slowly die of wounds suffered during World War I. Affected by humanity's inhumanity, he became fascinated with the animal world — studying zoology and animal behavior — and art. He became a curator of mammals at the London Zoo, and a television presenter. A surrealist painter himself, Morris even gave a paintbrush to a chimpanzee named Congo. The resulting work is said to have delighted Picasso. One chimp painting sold at auction for £14,400. In 1967 Morris wrote "The Naked Ape," a look at the evolution of man and how human behavior compared to that of other primates — including sexual selection and mating habits. "I spent the first half of my life studying animal behavior," Morris told The Guardian in 2007, "and when I eventually wrote a book about human beings, I wrote about them as if I was writing about another animal species. … I hadn't any hopes for it; I didn't expect it to do anything. People say I must have known what I was doing. They think I deliberately wrote it to make a shocking bestseller, but it wasn't like that." The book was a sensation, selling more than 20 million copies, but was also criticized as being patriarchal. Nearly four dozen books followed, including "The Human Zoo," "Intimate Behavior," "Manwatching" (about body language), "The Soccer Tribe," "Catwatching and Cat Lore," "Dogwatching," and "Babywatching." There were also books on surrealist art. "I should have stuck at the art," Morris told The Guardian. "I think I had the potential to be a good artist. I still consider myself a serious artist but a very minor one, and I'm a minor artist because I've been doing too many other things. My strength is that I do lots of different things; my weakness is that I don't stick at any of them long enough."

Bob Hall Bob Hall competes in the 1978 Boston Marathon. | Frank O'Brien/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Bob Hall (Oct. 31, 1951-April 12, 2026), who lost the use of his legs from polio during childhood, became known as the father of wheelchair racing, recognized as the Boston Marathon's Wheelchair Champion three times. Hall was not the first to compete in the Boston Marathon in a wheelchair; in 1970, Eugene Roberts, who'd lost both legs in the Vietnam War, completed the course, unsanctioned, in more than six hours. But in 1975, organizers promised Hall a finisher's certificate if he could complete the 26.2-mile distance in less than three hours. His finishing time: 2:58.00. "It had nothing to do with, per se, the marathon, but it was about the inclusion," Hall told The Associated Press last year, on the 50th anniversary of his pioneering ride. "It was that I was bringing people along." Hall won again in 1977 (at 2:40:18), besting seven fellow male and female wheelchair competitors, when Boston was designated the site for the National Wheelchair Championship. Hall received encouragement along the route from marathon winner Bill Rodgers and fifth-place finisher Tom Fleming, who both slowed to encourage him. "The interaction was a sign that we were fully accepted as athletes," he said. He sued in 1978 to have wheelchair racers admitted into the New York Marathon, where it would be more than two decades before men's and women's wheelchair divisions were created. Hundreds more wheelchair athletes have followed Hall, many using racing chairs he built. In Boston this year, 50 wheelchair racers competed, along with 50 others in para and adaptive divisions. "Because of him crossing that finish line, we're able to race today. And it's evolved so much since then," five-time Boston winner and eight-time Paralympic gold medalist Tatyana McFadden told The AP last year. "It was him. It was him being brave and saying, 'I'm going to go out and do this because I believe that we should be able to race Boston Marathon just like everyone else.' So he had the courage to do that."

Pearl Fryar Pearl Fryar in his topiary garden in Bishopville, S.C. in 2017. | Jonathan Newton/The Washington Post via Getty Images "The moment you work a cut above average, you will be recognized for that," self-taught topiary artist Pearl Fryar (Dec. 4, 1939-April 4, 2026) told "Sunday Morning" in 2005. "And I was a person that wanted some recognition in my lifetime." The recognition he initially sought, after he and his wife Metra moved into a ranch house in Lee County, S.C., was to win the local garden club's Yard of the Month Award, owing to his carefully landscaped and decorated front lawn and flower beds. It turned out Fryar wasn't even eligible; his house was outside Bishopville's city limits. But he didn't give up. "Now I got to come up with some way to make them make an exception, and that's how I got into topiary," he said. Fryar, who'd never heard the word "topiary," got a three-minute lesson from the owner of a local nursery on how to prune a plant. With a gas-powered hedge trimmer in his hands, Fryar was transformed — and so was his property. "Just started cutting everything I had in my garden," he said. "Pine trees, oak tree, it didn't make any difference, I started cutting." Out of a former cornfield he created a three-acre topiary garden, filled with plants and shaped into whimsical living sculptures — trees carved into fish, mushrooms and sailing ships. Hedgerows bubble up; plants twist and spiral towards one another. He carved the words "Love, Peace, and Goodwill" into the lawn. In January 1985, Fryar came home from work one day and found the sign reading, "Yard of the Month." "I went out screaming, because I had accomplished my goal," he said. "They left it for three months and they came out and they said to me, 'Well, we can't give it to you anymore because you're professional.'" Fryar's topiary garden, now overseen by a nonprofit organization, contains 400 topiaries, alongside junk art sculptures. It would take two weeks for the heralded "Picasso of Plants" to trim his whole garden — engaging in what he called "yard aerobics" — before starting all over again, all while also working at a beverage can manufacturing company. After his retirement (he said work interfered with his hobby), Fryar gave tours of the grounds, which attracted 10,000 visitors a year. And it had a spillover effect; Fryar's neighbors began shaping their landscapes, too, because, how could you not? The pleasure Fryar gave, and got back, made all the trouble worthwhile. "In my garden, you see a lot of love and hearts and 'I love you,' and I think one of the greatest things in the world is to say to someone `I love you,' you know? And in a sly way, that's what I have done."

Mary Beth Hurt Mary Beth Hurt as Helen in 1982's "The World According to Garp." | Warner Brothers Actress Mary Beth Hurt (Sept. 26, 1946-March 28, 2026) appeared in about two dozen New York productions, earning three Tony Award nominations for "Trelawny of the Wells," "Crimes of the Heart" and "Benefactors." An Iowa native (her babysitter was future actress Jean Seberg), Mary Beth Supinger studied at New York University's graduate theater program and performed in regional theaters, where she met her first husband, William Hurt. Upon graduation, she performed in West London with The Questors theater troupe, and in New York at Joseph Papp's Public Theater, starring in "As You Like It." She made her Broadway debut in 1974 in "Love for Love" — co-starring another actress making her Broadway debut, Glenn Close. She made her feature film debut in Woody Allen's drama "Interiors" (playing the sister of Diane Keaton and Kristin Griffth) and appeared in "The World According to Garp" (opposite Robin Williams), "Slaves of New York," "The Age of Innocence," "Six Degrees of Separation," "Autumn in New York" and other features. After divorcing William Hurt, she married film director Paul Schrader, and appeared in his films "Affliction" and "Light Sleeper." "I've never been extremely comfortable playing the lead in a play," Hurt told Theater Life in 2010. "I don't like the responsibility; there's a feeling that I have to be good. Besides, I found secondary parts much more interesting, especially when I was younger and the ingénue roles were pretty bland. I never felt very beautiful, or incredibly smart or witty, so I was always looking for something about them that intrigued me. And I would sort of twist that character in a way, because I remember thinking that an ingénue character doesn't ever think they're an ingénue. They think they're a person and they have idiosyncrasies. Those idiosyncrasies interested me." One lead role she did have on film: providing the voice of Jean Seberg, her childhood babysitter, in the 1995 biopic "From The Journals of Jean Seberg."

Dash Crofts Dash Crofts, of Seals & Crofts, performs at Georgia Tech's Alexander Memorial Coliseum, October 22, 1977 in Atlanta. | Tom Hill/WireImage via Getty Singer-songwriter Darrell "Dash" Crofts (Aug. 14, 1938-March 25, 2026) and Jim Seals were native West Texans and high school friends who had played together in various groups before teaming up as a duo, Seals & Crofts. Beginning in the late '60s, when they first opened for such acts as Chicago, Eric Clapton, and the Guess Who, Seals & Crofts' soft rock songs — blends of pop, country, jazz and folk — included such Top 10 hits as "Summer Breeze," "Diamond Girl" and "Get Closer." Other hits included "I'll Play for You," "Hummingbird," "We May Never Pass This Way (Again)," "Goodbye Old Buddies," and "You're the Love." Both had embraced the Baha'i faith, which advocated for global unity, and the religion's themes were woven into their music. "Some people have called it religious music," Crofts told Stereo Review in 1971. "It's not actually religious music, though it is inspired by religion. But no particular musical group influenced us, and I think that's one of the reasons that what is coming out is really us. … We've been in the hard rock scene for a long, long time, and we never mind hearing it and being around it. But playing it gets to be pretty tough physically after a while. … It's such a nice relief to just sit and play pretty stuff for a change." They created controversy with their 1974 anti-abortion ballad "Unborn Child," released the year after the Supreme Court's decision in Roe v. Wade. Although the album was certified gold, numerous radio stations refused to play the song, and protesters picketed. By the early 1980s, with soft-rock going out of fashion, Seals & Crofts were dropped by their label, and they broke up. In 1991 Crofts told the Los Angeles Times that he walked away from recording: "I was completely out of good material. What I had was so bad that we said: 'Why spend the money to go in and (record) this, knowing that nobody's going to like it, and we're not pleased with it?' If it isn't something you respond to yourself, you can't get that excited about doing it for others." But the two later reunited to tour, and in 2004 recorded the album "Traces." Crofts also recorded the 1998 solo album "Today." Jim Seals died in 2022. Crofts told the Times, "Lyrically, I think music can convey things that are hard sometimes for people to say to each other. But through a song, through someone else's eyes, they can see it and it's not so much a confrontation." Music also permeated their families. In the 1970s, Jim's brother, Dan Seals, teamed up with Croft's high school classmate, John Ford Coley, to record together as England Dan & John Ford Coley ("I'd Really Love to See You Tonight"). In 2010, Seal's daughter, Juliet Crossley, and Crofts' daughter, Amelia Dailey, formed a group called the Humming Birds. And in 2018, Seals' cousin Brady and Crofts' daughter Lua formed the duo Seals & Crofts 2.

Chip Taylor Chip Taylor performs at the 47th Annual Songwriters Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony, at the Marriott Marquis Hotel in New York, June 9, 2016. | Charles Sykes/Invision/AP Born James Wesley Voight (his brothers are Academy Award-winning actor Jon Voight, and world-famous geologist Barry Voight), musician and songwriter Chip Taylor (March 21, 1940-March 23, 2026) was best known for the songs made famous by others: "Wild Thing," recorded by The Troggs and Jimi Hendrix; "Angel of the Morning" by Merilee Rush and Juice Newton; "Try (Just a Little Bit Harder)" by Janis Joplin; and "I Can't Let Go" by The Hollies and Linda Ronstadt. "When I started writing hits, it was a very proud period of time that I had," he told "Sunday Morning" in 2001. "I mean, I loved the fact that other people would record my songs." But he wanted to record his own songs as well. Beginning in 1971, he released several solo albums, including "Chip Taylor's Last Chance," called one of the best country albums of the year by Rolling Stone. But seven years later, a dispute with his record label — when they refused to promote what he thought would be a hit single — led him to leave music and take up gambling, which had been a part-time hobby. For nearly 15 years, he called New York's Belmont Park home. Gambling became his muse, and his livelihood. "It was a fun job," he said. In the mid-1990s, he restarted his music career when his mother was dying of cancer. "My mom got very ill, and that was the real turning point," he said. "I decided one day instead of going to the racetrack to go down and play some songs for mom to make her feel a little better. So, I guess I missed [it] a little bit. Spending the real good quality time with my mom that one day gave me the spirit to do it the next day — not for Mom but for us, for Mom and me. … And I'd go up to my little recording studio, which had been left dormant for pretty much all the time, and I started recording a couple of things." After his mother's death, Taylor stuck with his music, releasing 25 albums beginning in 1996. He launched his own recording label, Train Wreck Records, and toured the U.S. and Europe. And while Taylor's songwriting gifts continued to be appreciated (in 2001 the reggae artist Shaggy released a new cover of "Angel of the Morning," which hit #1 on the Billboard Chart), his brother Jon Voight wondered at what cost: "Well, you had to know that he has a genius for gambling. You have to understand, there's a lot of talent there that is really being laid to waste now. I mean, there's nothing but songs, songs, songs. I mean, how many hours a day do you have to keep working on songs?"

Valerie Perrine A portrait of Valerie Perrine as Eve Teschmacher in the 1978 film "Superman." | Hulton Archive/Getty Images Fate and luck (good and bad) marked the trajectory of Academy Award-nominated actress Valerie Perrine (Sept. 3, 1943-March 23, 2026). In 1969, one month before her wedding, her fiancée, a gun collector, accidentally shot himself, fatally. Later that year, while working at the Stardust Hotel in Las Vegas as a topless dancer, she was invited to a party in L.A.'s Benedict Canyon, but bowed out when she could not get an understudy to perform for her. That party would be the site of the Manson Family murders, where Sharon Tate and Perrine's then-boyfriend, Jay Sebring, were murdered. Several years later, Perrine survived a small plane crash in the Pyrenees while traveling to the San Sebastian Film Festival. The tragedies and near-misses of her early years were bookended with a Parkinson's diagnosis that ended her acting areer — one that had seen her win BAFTA, Cannes Film Festival and New York Critics Circle awards for her performance in Bob Fosse's "Lenny," playing the wife of comedian Lenny Bruce. She earned a best actress Oscar nomination for the role as well. Born in Galveston, Texas, her Army dad brought Valerie and her mother, a showgirl, to Japan. There, at age 4, Valerie began performing with a ceremonial dance troupe. But after relocating to Arizona, the family finances suffered, and Valerie left for Las Vegas at 17. "I wanted to show off," she told the Hollywood Reporter in 2023. Afte working as a showgirl, she transitioned to acting, making her film debut in 1971's "Slaughterhouse-Five," based on the Kurt Vonnegut novel, and appearing in several TV movies before landing "Lenny." She was best known as Eve Teschmacher, the assistant to arch villain Lex Luthor, in the first two "Superman" films opposite Christopher Reeve. Perrine, who was afraid of water, said that she'd drunk "a whole bottle of champagne" before filming a scene in which she dives into a pool to rescue, then kiss, the drowning Man of Steel. "I'm a desert girl," she explained. Other credits included "W.C. Fields and Me," "The Magician of Lublin," "The Electric Horseman," "Can't Stop the Music," "The Border," "Maid to Order," "Bright Angel," "Sweet Bird of Youth," and "What Women Want," as well as TV appearances including "Northern Exposure," "Burke's Law," "Homicide: Life on the Street," "ER," "Nash Bridges," "The Practice," "Walker, Texas Ranger," "As the World Turns" and other series. The 2019 documentary "Valerie," directed by her longtime friend Stacey Souther, traces her life and the Parkinson's that robbed her of much mobility. "No matter what life gives you, you have to fight," she said. But she did not sound regretful: "I think I've done it all."

Robert Mueller Former Special Counsel Robert Mueller testifies before Congress about the Russia-Trump investigation, on July 24, 2019. | Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Robert Mueller (Aug. 7, 1944-March 20, 2026), a former Marine, served as a United States attorney, deputy attorney general, and director of the FBI. He investigated white collar crimes, bank fraud, and state-sponsored terrorism, and led prosecutions of mob boss John Gotti, Panamanian leader Manuel Noriega, and the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103. But his most high-profile role was as a special counsel, tasked to investigate Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and its possible connections with the campaign of President Trump. His probe, which was completed in 2019, operated under restrictions imposed by a White House legal counsel opinion that a sitting president could not face criminal charges. Mueller, however, reiterated that a president could be charged once he'd left office. His team did not depose Mr. Trump, however, fearful that court fights over a subpoena would have delayed the investigation further. Mr. Trump claimed that the report, released in a redacted form in the spring of 2019, cleared him of wrongdoing. However, Mueller wrote in an introduction about whether Mr. Trump had obstructed justice: "If we had confidence after a thorough investigation of the facts that the President clearly did not commit obstruction of justice we would so state. … [W]hile this report does not conclude that the President committed a crime, it also does not exonerate him." Federal charges were levied against 34 people, including 25 Russian nationals, and three Russian companies. In his report, Mueller wrote that while the evidence did not establish that Mr. Trump was involved in an underlying crime, "the evidence does point to a range of other possible personal motives animating the President's conduct. These include concerns that continued investigation would call into question the legitimacy of his election and potential uncertainty about whether certain events—such as advance notice of WikiLeaks's release of hacked information or the June 9, 2016 meeting between senior campaign officials and Russians—could be seen as criminal activity by the President, his campaign, or his family." He added, "The President launched public attacks on the investigation and individuals involved in it who could possess evidence adverse to the President, while in private, the President engaged in a series of targeted efforts to control the investigation." In July 2019, Mueller was called to testify before congressional panels. He merely reiterated the report's findings – that the investigation did find that "the Russian government interfered in the 2016 presidential election in sweeping and systematic fashion," through disinformation and document leaks whose goal was "supporting the Trump campaign and disparaging candidate Hillary Clinton." Mueller did confirm that Trump campaign officials (including Carter Page, George Papadopoulos, Michael Flynn, Donald Trump Jr., Jared Kushner and Paul Manafort) all had contacts with Russians. However, he did not establish that they "conspired or coordinated" with the Russian government. Regarding a June 2016 meeting at Trump Tower in New York City, during which Donald Trump Jr., Paul Manafort and Jared Kushner discussed the release of potentially damaging information about Clinton with a Russian lawyer, Mueller said he could not prove the participants knew their conduct was illegal at the time the meeting took place. He said shifting explanations about why the meeting took place had been made to "avoid political consequences." Republicans called the FBI's investigation into Trump's ties with Russia, which had predated Mueller's probe, politically motivated, accusations Mueller denied, calling the investigation and the people who conducted it "fair and independent." He chose to let the report speak for itself, and rarely gave interviews. But in 2024, he provided the introduction to a book, "Interference: The Inside Story of Trump, Russia, and the Mueller Investigation," written by lawyers who'd served on his team. "The evidence was clear that the Russian government engaged in multiple, systematic attacks designed to undermine our democracy and favor one candidate over the other," Mueller wrote. "We were not prepared then and, despite many efforts of dedicated people across the government, we are not prepared now. This threat deserves the attention of every American. Russia attacked us before and will do so again."

Chuck Norris Chuck Norris in the TV series "Walker, Texas Ranger," in 1997. | CBS via Getty Images Martial arts grandmaster and action hero Chuck Norris (March 10, 1940-March 19, 2026) started his training in judo and Tang Soo Do while deployed with the Air Force as an MP in Korea. He became a six-time undefeated world professional middleweight karate champion and launched a movie and TV career that spanned more than 30 action films and the long-running CBS series "Walker, Texas Ranger." After receiving his honorable discharge in 1962, Norris worked at Northrop Aircraft as a clerk and opened a martial arts studio in Redondo Beach, Calif. He developed his own Korean-based American hard style of karate, known sometimes as Chun Kuk Do. The studio became a chain. One student, Steve McQueen, encouraged him to get into acting. After an uncredited role as a bodyguard in the Dean Martin film "The Wrecking Crew," he received his first credited role in the Hong Kong martial arts film "The Way of the Dragon," opposite Bruce Lee, followed by "Yellow-Face Tiger," playing a San Francisco drug lord. He was then top-billed in a string of popular movies, including "Breaker! Breaker!," "Good Guys Wear Black," "A Force of One," "The Octagon," "An Eye for an Eye," "Forced Vengeance," "Lone Wolf McQuade," "Missing in Action," "Code of Silence," and "The Delta Force." Meanwhile, in the late 1970s he'd founded the United Fighting Arts Federation. In 1985 he told CBS News' "West 57th," "Think of this: Here I was, a kid who never excelled in any sports in school. I was too small. So, I get into karate and I become a world karate champion. Here's a kid who could not even get in front of a class and give a book report, all the way through school, and now I'm an actor." For nine seasons, beginning in 1993, he starred in the CBS series "Walker, Texas Ranger," which he described to the Associated Press as "fighting injustice with justice, good vs. bad." He followed the advice of McQueen, who'd told him, "Don't talk unless there's something to say." "I don't like dialogue that much anyway," Norris told CBS. "It's not in me to be a Dustin Hoffman or a Laurence Olivier. I enjoy the action, because I'm physical. And I enjoy the basic heroic image that I project, that I think is a good image for kids to see. "The difference between violence and action is the philosophy when you use it," he said. "What I mean there is, if I provoke something, and I get into a physical thing because I've provoked it, I consider that violent. But if I'm put into a position where I have no way of getting out of it except through action or fighting, then there's a certain philosophy there, because the kids say, 'Well, he didn't look for it.'" While his "tough guy" image made him an icon, it also sparked internet parodies. The viral "Chuck Norris Facts" posed absurd statements alluding to Norris' tough-guy image, such as "When the Boogeyman goes to sleep every night, he checks his closet for Chuck Norris;" and "Chuck Norris can slam a revolving door." He ultimately embraced the ridiculousness of the memes and penned "The Official Chuck Norris Fact Book," which raised money for a nonprofit (co-founded with President George H.W. Bush) to promote martial arts instruction for children. "To some who know little of my martial arts or film careers but perhaps grew up with 'Walker, Texas Ranger,' it seems that I have become a somewhat mythical superhero icon," he wrote. "I am flattered and humbled." In 2012 Norris joined fellow action movie stars Sylvester Stallone, Arnold Schwarzenegger, Bruce Willis, Jet Li and Jean-Claude Van Damme in "The Expendables 2." With a wink to his internet memes, Norris' character, a retired military operative named Booker, confirmed that he'd once been bitten by a king cobra: "But after five days of agonizing pain, the cobra died."

Alexander Butterfield White House aide Alexander Butterfield at the swearing-in before the Senate Watergate Committee in July 1973. | Steve Northup/Getty Images In July 1973, White House aide Alexander Butterfield (April 6, 1926-March 9, 2026) gave dramatic testimony to a Senate committee investigating Watergate. When asked if he was aware of any listening devices in the Oval Office, Butterfield replied, "I was aware of listening devices, yes, sir." Butterfield, who served as deputy assistant to President Nixon, actually oversaw the secret, voice-activated taping system that was installed in the White House, in Nixon's office in the Executive Office Building, and at the presidential retreat at Camp David. According to Butterfield, it was known only to himself, Nixon, chief of staff H.R. Haldeman (an old college friend of Butterfield's) and several Secret Service agents. Washington Post reporter Bob Woodward had tried and failed to interview Butterfield, and so he passed his name on to the Congressional committee, who brought him in to testify. Woodward told "Sunday Morning" in 2015 that, had Butterfield not revealed the recording system documenting Richard Nixon's coverup of the break-in at the Democratic National Committee Headquarters, it might never have become known. The revelation of the White House tapes, implicating Nixon, led to the president's resignation. Butterfield accepted that his admission presaged the president's fall. "I didn't like to be the cause of that, but I felt that I was, in a lot of ways," he said in a 2008 oral history for the Nixon Presidential Library and Museum. After Butterfield retired to California, he offered Woodward 20 boxes of notes and materials he'd taken from his days at the White House. He also sat for 40 hours of interviews, which became the basis of Woodward's 2015 book, "The Last of the President's Men." That book would become a beacon for Cassidy Hutchinson, a young Trump White House aide, who, in 2022, was called to testify before the Congressional committee investigating Jan. 6 and the president's actions during the assault on the Capitol. Hutchinson, who said she struggled with the thought of betraying her coworkers, ultimately dropped her legal representation (paid for by a Trump PAC) and testified before Congress. Hutchinson, who later befriended Butterfield, told "Sunday Morning" that his experience during and after Watergate "really was the source of strength for me, and gave me the perspective not only that I could do this, but that there was life on the other side of it." Asked by "Sunday Morning" if he would do anything differently with regard to revealing the Nixon taping system, Butterfield replied, "No, I've thought of that a lot. I regret absolutely nothing. I didn't do everything right. But I satisfied myself that I didn't tell a lie."

"Country Joe" McDonald "Country Joe" McDonald performs with Country Joe and the Fish during the Schaefer Music Festival in New York City's Central Park in 1968. | Harvey L. Silver/Corbis via Getty Images A longtime presence in the Bay Area music scene whose peers included the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane, and Big Brother and the Holding Company, rock star "Country Joe" McDonald (Jan. 1, 1942 – March 7, 2026) wrote or co-wrote hundreds of songs, and was a founding member of Country Joe and the Fish. Attending college in L.A. following three years in the Navy, McDonald met banjo/guitar player Blair Hardman, and their shared love of folk music figures like Woody Guthrie led McDonald to learn guitar. They recorded an album, "The Goodbye Blues." Moving to Berkeley, he teamed up with Barry "The Fish" Melton, and as Country Joe and the Fish released nearly a dozen albums and EPs, blending protest songs, folk and psychedelic rock, with openly political content. McDonald would become best known for his 1965 song, "I-Feel-Like-I'm-Fixin'-To-Die Rag," which he performed during Woodstock in 1969. It became an anthem for Vietnam War protesters: And it's one, two, three,

what are we fighting for?

Don't ask me, I don't give a damn

Next stop is Vietnam.

And it's five, six, seven,

open up the pearly gates,

Well, there ain't no time to wonder why,

Whoopee! We're all gonna die! The song originally opened with McDonald leading the audience in a four-letter cheer ("F-I-S-H"). Gradually, that chant became a different four-letter word, which led to a cancelled appearance on "The Ed Sullivan Show" and an arrest and fine for using the cheer at a concert in Worcester, Mass. When he was called as a witness in the trial of the Chicago Seven, he even began performing the song on the stand. The judge interrupted, telling McDonald, "No singing is permitted in the courtroom." He recited the words instead. When the group disbanded, McDonald continued writing protest songs for different wars ("Support the Troops" was written in response to the Iraq War), as well as on such themes as the environment ("Save the Whales," "Blood on the Ice"), hunting ("Wilderness Trail"), and onetime girlfriend Janis Joplin ("Janis"). His albums included "Thinking of Woody Guthrie," "War War War," "Country Joe," "Paradise With an Ocean View," "Superstition Blues," "Carry On," "Time Flies By" and "50." He also made appearances in movies (including the 1971 "psychedelic western" "Zachariah"), and wrote music for the Danish film "Quiet Days in Clichy," based on a Henry Miller novel. He had an affinity for nurses ("Lady with the Lamp"), and even dedicated a portion of his website to Florence Nightingale. For nurses serving during the war and caring for veterans, he composed "The Girl Next Door": She grew up in America, just the girl next door

Never thought to question what we were fighting for

They sent her off to war and showed her death and pain

And the girl next door will never be the same … She's everybody's savior but her own,

the Army combat nurse,

but who will save her now? "I'm sort of the Greek chorus," he told The Street Spirit in 2016. "I just ask these questions, and give a voice to people who don't have a voice." McDonald was conflicted about his anti-war music. The son of parents who were ardent Communists, he'd served in the Navy in Japan, and identified both with protesters and the military serving overseas. He stood, dressed in Navy whites, alongside members of Vietnam Veterans Against the War in Washington, D.C. He also helped organize the construction of a Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Berkeley, which was unveiled in 1995.

Neil Sedaka Singer-songwriter Neil Sedaka performing in 1986. | Keystone/Hulton Archive/Getty Images Singer-songwriter Neil Sedaka (March 13, 1939-Feb. 27, 2026) composed songs of love, longing and broken hearts in a career that spanned generations. His songs included the Billboard #1 hits "Bad Blood," "Breaking Up Is Hard to Do," and "Laughter in the Rain," while he also wrote songs recorded by the likes of Frank Sinatra, Elvis Presley and Cher. Sedaka's rollercoaster career seems appropriate, given he grew up just down the boardwalk from Coney Island, in Brooklyn's Brighton Beach. His musical education began early. When he was 8, a schoolteacher – recognizing his talent – persuaded Sedaka's parents to buy him a second-hand piano. And he had dreams of success. "I used to buy the little 45 records," he told "Sunday Morning" in 2007, "and with a pen, I would scratch out the name of the artist and the songwriter and write down 'Neil Sedaka' to see how it looked." At age 9, Sedaka received a scholarship to the Juilliard School of Music; he studied there through two years of college. But while playing the classics, he also formed a doo-wop group, The Tokens, with classmates from Brooklyn's Abraham Lincoln High School. He recorded two hit singles with them, including "While I Dream." Sedaka teamed with a neighborhood friend, Howie Greenfield, and became one of the most successful songwriting duos of all time. Their first hit, recorded by Connie Francis, was "Stupid Cupid," which hit #14 on the charts in 1958. And he was prolific. By his count, Sedaka wrote more than a thousand songs, including 30 Billboard 100 hits. Between 1958 and 1963, Sedaka sold 40 million records, with such songs as "Oh, Carol" (a tribute to his high school girlfriend Carole King), "Calendar girl," "Happy Birthday, Sweet Sixteen," "The Diary," "You Mean Everything To Me," and "The Dreamer." "It was mind-blowing," he said. "To turn on the radio, I was riding my Chevy Impala, 1959, white convertible with the fins, and I pushed three buttons on my car radio and I heard "Oh Carol" on three stations at the same time. It was like a dream." And then came The Beatles. The British invasion changed the pop landscape. Sedaka stopped singing, but his songs continued to be sung by other artists, including Tom Jones, Elvis Presley, Frank Sinatra, The Monkees, and The Fifth Dimension. Sedaka moved to England, which is where he met Elton John, who signed Sedaka to his new label, Rocket Records, and in late 1974, he released the album, "Sedaka's Back." The single "Laughter in the Rain" became Sedaka's signature tune, while his song "Love Will Keep Us Together," became a monster hit for The Captain and Tennille. Sedaka continued performing into his 80s, and in 2007 released an album, "The Definitive Collection," that debuted at #22 on the Billboard charts. In 2020 "Sunday Morning" asked Sedaka what makes a pop hit. "There are various notes that go with various chords," he replied. "And if the sentiment is right, it gives you that … in the groin, in the heart. You get those chills." And he made it so that his music was reachable. "I write vocally," Sedaka said. "Usually not more than an octave and a couple of notes, so that it's singable. You can write songs that everyone knows, but you can't write songs that everyone sings."

Willie Colón Salsa musician Willie Colon performs at Gran Forum on July 1, 2017 in Mexico City. | Pedro Gonzalez Castillo/LatinContent via Getty Images Musician and social activist Willie Colón (April 28, 1950-Feb. 21, 2026) was a trombonist, composer, arranger and singer who blended jazz and rock with classic Latin rhythms. An original talent in urban salsa, he recorded more than 40 albums over a six-decade career, selling more than 30 million copies worldwide. Nominated for 10 Grammys and one Latin Grammy, he collaborated with a wide range of artists, including the Fania All Stars, Héctor Lavoe, David Byrne, Ismael Miranda and Celia Cruz. His 1978 album "Siembra," with Rubén Blades, was named by Rolling Stone the best salsa album of all time. Born in the Bronx, Colón studied a variety of instruments from a young age, from the flute and bugle, to the trumpet and, finally, trombone. He began recording at age 16 for Fania Records, which was largely responsible for the burgeoning genre of salsa — a fusion of jazz, rock, funk, soul and R&B with old-school Cuban and Puerto Rican sounds such as Cuban son, cha-cha-cha, mambo, guaracha, jíbara and plena music. In 2004 he received a special lifetime Grammy from the Latin Recording Academy. Colón also fought for civil rights, and was part of various community groups, including the Hispanic Arts Association, the Latino Commission on AIDS, the Arthur Schomburg Coalition for a Better New York and the Congressional Hispanic Caucus Institute. He ran unsuccessfully for Congress in a 1994 Democratic primary. He told The New York Times that he was seeking other challenges. "Sometimes writing a song is not enough," he said.

Eric Dane Actor Eric Dane photographed at the St. Regis in Washington, D.C., Sept. 30, 2025. | Marvin Joseph/The Washington Post via Getty Images Actor Eric Dane (Nov. 9, 1972-Feb. 19, 2026) rose to fame playing Dr. Mark Sloan in the medical drama "Grey's Anatomy," a popular character dubbed "McSteamy." He later became an advocate for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) awareness and research, after being diagnosed with the condition, which is also known as Lou Gehrig's disease. Born and raised in Northern California, Dane moved to Los Angeles after high school to pursue acting. He earned credits on "Saved by the Bell," "Married...With Children," "Charmed," "Gideon's Crossing," and "X-Men: The Last Stand." What was initially a guest appearance on "Grey's Anatomy" turned into a regular role that lasted seven seasons, before his character died from injuries suffered in a plane crash. Beginning in 2019, he starred as Cal Jacobs in the HBO drama "Euphoria." After announcing his ALS diagnosis last year, he shot scenes for the show's third season in a wheelchair. He also made a guest appearance as a firefighter trying to hide his ALS diagnosis on the drama "Brilliant Minds." Other credits include "Valentine's Day," "Burlesque," "The Last Ship," "The Fixer," and "Countdown." A memoir, "Book of Days," is scheduled to be published in late 2026. "I want to capture the moments that shaped me," Dane said in a statement about the book. "The beautiful days, the hard ones, the ones I never took for granted, so that if nothing else, people who read it will remember what it means to live with heart."

Rev. Jesse Jackson The Rev. Jesse Jackson speaks during his 1984 presidential campaign in Chicago. | David Hume Kennerly/Getty Images A protégé of Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and an enthralling orator, Rev. Jesse Jackson (Oct. 8, 1941-Feb. 17, 2026) was an integral part of the civil rights movement, a stirring voice for economic justice and a trailblazing presidential candidate. His runs for the White House in the 1980s, and efforts promoting voter registration, helped set the stage for another politician from Chicago years later, Barack Obama. Jackson started out as a staff member of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. An ordained Baptist minister, he joined the voting rights march that King led from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama. King then sent Jackson to Chicago to launch Operation Breadbasket, which pressured companies to hire Black workers. Jackson was with King on April 4, 1968, when the civil rights leader was assassinated. In 1971, Jackson broke with the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and founded the civil rights organizations PUSH (later the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition) and PUSH Excel in Chicago — groups focused on education and programs designed to secure jobs for Black Americans and business for Black-owned companies. PUSH used lawsuits, and threats of boycotts, to pressure corporations to commit to diversifying their workforces. In the 1980s, he pursued the highest political office in the nation. He told "Sunday Morning" in 1984 about the desire for common ground — what he called a rainbow vote. "There are many levels where the interests of Blacks, Hispanics, women, teenagers, peace activists, unemployed people, our interests converge, and we must always struggle, it seems to me, to move from racial battleground and polarization to economic common ground," he said. "This is not a struggle for Blacks only. The industrial collapse of auto, steel, electronics, rubber and textile was not Blacks only. The need for a new fuel policy is not for Blacks only. This cry for health and education to be served based upon need, not just based upon wealth, is not Blacks only. So, I think that the coalition is being underestimated." And even before he entered the Democratic Party's presidential nomination process, Jackson saw beyond the immediacy of a run for the Oval Office: "The energy that we're organizing now is not just focused on the White House," he said. "It's focused on every level of government. We'll be able to translate the energy of this national enthusiasm into higher voter registration, more participation, more coalition. We're not talking about just a person running; we're talking about many people running for Congress and state legislature and supervisor and sheriff and registrar and tax assessor and school board. We're not talking about a kind of one-horse race." He achieved a few Democratic primary wins during his 1984 run — the first African American candidate to do so. Jackson's statements in support of the Palestinian Liberation Organization drew critics, while his challenging of establishment Democrats was also met with resistance. But in 1988, when Jackson mounted another run, almost 7 million Democratic voters picked him in the primaries and caucuses. He won 12 states, including Michigan and Virginia. (The nomination ultimately went to Massachusetts Gov. Michael Dukakis.) Even as his health faltered in later years, Jackson continued to speak out against racial injustice. He appeared at the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, and supported a resolution backing a ceasefire in the Israeli-Hamas war. He was also a voice in the Black Lives Matter demonstrations. "Even if we win," he told protesters in Minneapolis during the murder trial of the officer who was eventually convicted in the death of George Floyd, "it's relief, not victory. They're still killing our people. Stop the violence, save the children. Keep hope alive."

Frederick Wiseman Documentary filmmaker Frederick Wiseman photographed in Cambridge, Mass., June 11, 1969. | Elizabeth Jones/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Filmmaker Frederick Wiseman (Jan. 1, 1930-Feb 16, 2026) helped redefine the art of documentaries, with a style that encompassed long, observational studies of institutions and people, usually without voiceover narration, and shot as unobtrusively as possible. His subjects covered a vast range of society: a suburban high school, a horse racing track, a mental institution, the New York Public Library, a modeling agency, a Boston hospital, a juvenile court, meat production, a boxing gym, a 3-Michelin star restaurant. With no narrative devices imposed, Wiseman's leisurely films — many tip the scales at three, four, even six hours in length, edited down from hundreds of hours of footage — allow his subjects to speak for themselves, without the director passing judgments. Wiseman told "Sunday Morning," "One of the things I'm trying to do in having done a group of movies is to show as many different aspects of human behavior as I can." After studying law and producing the 1963 drama "The Cool World," Wiseman was in his mid-30s when he directed his first feature, the scandalous 1967 film "Titicut Follies," which he shot inside the Bridgewater State Hospital for the criminally insane in Massachusetts. The film, which depicts the abuse inmates suffered from sadistic guards, was screened at the New York Film Festival, but Massachusetts officials were successful in obtaining an injunction, claiming the privacy rights of the inmates had been violated. A judge ordered all copies of the film destroyed, but Wiseman won on appeal, though he was prohibited from showing the film outside of medical, legal or other related professional groups. In the 1990s a Superior Court judge allowed the film's general release on First Amendment grounds, and it was aired on PBS. It has since been selected for the Library of Congress' National Film Registry. In "High School" (1968), Wiseman recorded life in a suburban Philadelphia school, including an awkward sex education class. Other documentaries — "Hospital," "Public Housing," "Basic Training," "Boxing Gym" — were uncanny in how they invited viewers into the mindsets of the people captured on film. "The institution is also just an excuse to observe human behavior in somewhat defined conditions," Wiseman told The Associated Press in 2020. "The films are as much about that as they are about institutions." His films could be despairing or hopeful. "I think it's as important to document kindness, civility and generosity of spirit as it is to show cruelty, banality and indifference," Wiseman said when he accepted an honorary Academy Award in 2016. His film career had evolved after being drafted into the Army in 1955. Stationed in Paris, he began shooting street scenes with an 8mm camera. "I reached the witching age of 30 and figured I better do something I liked," Wiseman told the AP in 2016. "It was just a few years after the technological developments that it made it possible to shoot synchronous sound ... so that opened up the world for filmmaking. And there were so many good subjects that hadn't been filmed, as there still are."

Master Sergeant Juan Valdez Master Sgt. Juan Valdez (pictured rear) was the last Marine out of Saigon when the city fell on April 30, 1975. | Photo courtesy of Juan Valdez On April 30, 1975, as Saigon fell to the approaching North Vietnamese army, a massive evacuation was ongoing from the capital and surrounding area. At the U.S. Embassy compound, helicopters ferried more than 900 Americans, 1,120 Vietnamese, and third-country nationals to ships offshore. A Marine detachment, led by Master Sergeant Juan Valdez (1938-Feb 15, 2026), helped protect the operation. Born in San Antonio to second-generation Mexican immigrants, Valdez joined the Marine Corps after high school, and served his first tour of duty in Vietnam beginning in 1965. He returned to the States and became a Company First Sergeant at Camp Pendleton, but in 1974 he was sent to Saigon as commander of the U.S. Embassy's Marine Corps forces. But once American personnel were cleared from the Embassy during Saigon's fall, Valdez's Marine detachment, which had locked down elevators and barricaded the last door, were on the roof, finding that the last helicopter had departed without them. "We thought for sure that we were going to be left there," Valdez told "Sunday Morning" in 2025. "You kind of swallow hard, you know, because by that time the tanks were passing by from the Vietnamese." The compound walls were breached. But then, a CH-46 helicopter appeared to pick up the remaining Marines. Once it landed, Valdez ordered all remaining Marines onto the aircraft. It took off without him. When a headcount was taken, the helicopter was ordered to the roof again, and three Marines grabbed Valdez and pulled him on board. "I was the last one to go aboard," said Valdez. "Because I was in charge of them, and whether I stayed behind, so be it, you know, but you always take care of your men first." He was the last American out of Saigon.

Robert Duvall Robert Duvall in his Oscar-nominated performance as Lt. Col. Kilgore in Francis Ford Coppola's "Apocalypse Now." | Zoetrope/Paramount Pictures via Getty Images One of the best actors of his generation, Robert Duvall (Jan. 5, 1931-Feb. 15, 2026) starred in such classics as "The Godfather" and "The Godfather Part II," "M*A*S*H," "Apocalypse Now," and "Tender Mercies," for which he won the Academy Award. In a career spanning nearly seven decades, Duvall was noted for his understated performances, subsuming himself into characters that manifested moral conflicts or ethical struggles — most notably as Tom Hagen, the Corleone family's consigliere, in the first two "Godfather" films; Mac Sledge, a country singer seeking to redeem himself, in "Tender Mercies"; and as Boo Radley, a shy man who befriends young Scout, in the 1962 adaptation of "To Kill a Mockingbird." But Duvall could also go large, such as his full-throttle performance as Lt. Col. Kilgore in "Apocalypse Now," who leads a helicopter attack on a Vietnamese village in order to secure a safe zone for surfing; Bull Meechum, the overbearing Marine pilot and father in "The Great Santini"; and Frank Hackett, a corporate TV executive who runs roughshod over a news division in "Network." Even in small parts, he could steal a movie. In 2004, he explained to "60 Minutes" that, whether his characters were heroic or villainous, down-to-earth or tenacious, there's a bit of Robert Duvall in all of them. "Has to be. It's you underneath," he said. "You interpret somebody. You try to let it come from yourself." The son of a Navy rear admiral, Duvall studied acting in New York alongside Gene Hackman, Dustin Hoffman and James Caan, and after some early TV roles, he made his film debut in "To Kill a Mockingbird." In "M*A*S*H," Robert Altman's 1970 satire of war, Duvall played Major Frank Burns, a by-the-book Army surgeon whose religious zeal didn't get in the way of his having an affair with the hospital's chief nurse, "Hot Lips" Houlihan (Sally Kellerman). Burns becomes a foil and butt of jokes of other doctors at the M*A*S*H unit, until he is literally driven into a straitjacket Duvall followed with a lead role in "THX 1138," a science fiction film directed by one of Coppola's friends, George Lucas. But an even bigger role was Duvall's supporting turn in Coppola's "The Godfather." Cast opposite Marlon Brando, James Caan and Al Pacino, Duvall played an Irish lawyer who had been "adopted" into the Corleone family — his sole client. Balancing the wishes of Brando's Vito Corleone, the hot-headed antics of Caan's Sonny, and the resistance of Pacino's Michael, Tom Hagen was a tested voice of reason, a deliverer of bad news, and an instrument of revenge. He repeated the role in "The Godfather Part II." But when Coppola went to film Part III of his gangster saga, Duvall and the studio couldn't come to terms on salary, and so Tom Hagen was killed off. One of his most celebrated roles was in Coppola's "Apocalypse Now," playing Lt. Col. Kilgore, who heads a helicopter attack on a suspected Viet Cong village, blaring Wagner on loudspeakers. Kilgore's bare-chested speech ("I love the smell of napalm in the morning … it smells like victory"), as a forest is incinerated nearby, articulated the brutality and insanity of war, and became one of cinema's iconic moments. Duvall took his role seriously, even as explosives were discharged all around him. "I played a guy that didn't flinch, so I didn't flinch. You know what I mean?" he told Esquire magazine in 2014. "I played that kind of guy — a non-flinching guy. If you flinch when the script says not to flinch, you should be fired." For "Tender Mercies," playing an alcoholic country singer trying to make a spiritual and professional comeback, he sang every song himself. "They were trying to get around it," Duvall told "Sunday Morning" in 2006, "but I said, 'No, no. This has to be part of it. You cannot dub [another singer] later. I have to do that.'" Duvall had said his favorite role was Gus McCrae, the Texas Ranger turned-philosopher cowboy, in the 1989 TV miniseries "Lonesome Dove." He directed three films: "Angelo, My Love"; "The Apostle," in which he played a Pentecostal preacher on the run from the law; and "Assassination Tango," which was his tribute to Argentine dance. The qualities of Duvall's work, from the histrionic to the silent, were evident in the naturalness of his delivery. As he said to "Sunday Morning," "What makes what I do work? It's this, what we're doing right now: talking and listening. … That's the beginning and the end. The beginning and the end is to be simple."

James Van Der Beek Actor James Van Der Beek in a publicity photo for the 1999 film "Varsity Blues." | Getty Images James Van Der Beek (March 8, 1977-Feb. 11, 2026) became a star, at age 20, as the lead in the drama series "Dawson's Creek," playing Dawson Leery, a teenager and aspiring filmmaker in a budding romantic relationship with a neighbor, Joey (played by Katie Holmes). The show, chronicling the ups-and-downs of their romance, ran on The WB for six seasons. "It's tough to compete with something that was the cultural phenomenon that 'Dawson's Creek' was," he told Vulture in 2013. "It ran for so long. That's a lot of hours playing one character in front of people. So, it's natural that they associate you with that." Raised in Cheshire, Connecticut, Van Der Beek began acting after suffering a concussion playing football at 13, and starred in a school production of "Grease." He landed an off-Broadway role, at age 16, in Edward Albee's "Finding the Sun." He also appeared in a revival of the musical "Shenandoah" at the Goodspeed Opera House. Post-"Dawson's Creek" credits included "Varsity Blues," "Texas Rangers," "The Rules of Attraction," "One Tree Hill," "Mercy," "Downsizing," "Jay and Silent Bob Strike Back," "How I Met Your Mother," "CSI: Cyber," and "Criminal Minds." He also appeared in Funny Or Die videos, and in the Viceland mockumentary satire "What Would Diplo Do?" "The more you make fun of yourself and don't try to go for any kind of respect, the more people seem to respect you," he told Vanity Fair in 2011. "I've always been a clown trapped in a leading man's body."

Bud Cort Bud Cort and Ruth Gordon in the 1971 comedy "Harold and Maude." | John Springer Collection/Corbis via Getty Images Character actor Bud Cort (March 29, 1948-Feb. 11, 2026) was most famous for a role he played in his youth, in the 1971 cult hit "Harold and Maude," Hal Ashby's dark comedy about a morbid young man who begins a relationship with a geriatric free spirit (played by Ruth Gordon). The quirky romance earned him Golden Globe and BAFTA nominations. Born Walter Cox, he adopted a stage name courtesy of New York's Cort Theatre. He appeared in films by Robert Altman ("MASH," "Brewster McCloud"), Michael Mann ("Heat"), Wes Anderson ("The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou"), Tobe Hooper ("Invaders From Mars"), Ed Harris ("Pollack"), and Keith Gordon ("The Chocolate War"). His career was disrupted by a near-fatal car crash in 1979, when he suffered multiple fractures, facial lacerations and a concussion. Cort was the voice of a computer in the comedy "Electric Dreams," Sigmund Freud in "The Secret Diary of Sigmund Freud," and God in Kevin Smith's "Dogma." In 1991 he directed, co-wrote, and starred in "Ted and Venus." Other credits included "And the Band Played On," "Arrested Development," "Ugly Betty," and "Criminal Minds." In 2010 he talked with The New York Times about how his role as the death-obsessed Harold Chasen became something of a curse: "I didn't make a film for five years because everything I was offered was that same kind of a character," he said. "Because I worked so hard on that performance, everyone assumed I was that person. I've been through the whole thing of being followed around. People used to come to my hotel and leave tombstones and pictures of dead babies. I try to talk to them, tell them they missed the point of the movie."

Demond Wilson Demond Wilson, star of the 1970s sitcom "Sanford and Son." | NBCUniversal via Getty Images Demond Wilson (Oct. 13, 1946-Jan. 30, 2026) was best known for playing Redd Foxx's son Lamont on "Sanford and Son" in the early 1970s. Adapated by Norman Lear from the British comedy "Steptoe and Son," about a grumpy and irascible junk man and his aspirational adult offspring, "Sanford and Son" was one of the earliest American sitcoms to feature a predominantly Black cast, and was for many years NBC's top-rated show. Born in Valdosta, Georgia, Wilson grew up in Harlem. As a child he appeared on radio and danced on the stage of the Apollo Theatre. As a teenager, a ruptured appendix led him to promise to devote himself to God. He was wounded while serving with the Army in Vietnam, and upon his return to New York began acting off-Broadway, before going to Hollywood. After a guest role on Lear's "All in the Family," he was hired for one of the leads in "Sanford and Son." In 2022, Wilson told the Associated Press that he was competing with Richard Pryor for the role opposite Foxx. "I said, 'C'mon, you can't put a comedian with a comedian. You've got to have a straight man,'" he said he told producers. Debuting in 1972, the show ran on NBC for six seasons, and spent most of its run in the Nielsen Top 10 (frequently second only to Lear's "All in the Family"). The series ended when ABC lured Foxx away to host his own variety show. Wilson later starred in the TV shows "Baby I'm Back" and "The New Odd Couple" (playing Oscar Madison). He also appeared in "Girlfriends" and the film "The Organization." But he did not find acting fulfilling, and in the 1980s he became an ordained minister. "Show business did not come out of me. I came out of show business," he told Jet Magazine in 1985. He also founded Restoration House of America, an organization that helps rehabilitate prison inmates and the formerly incarcerated, and wrote several books, including children's stories.

Catherine O'Hara Catherine O'Hara attends a sneak peek of "Schitt's Creek" during the 11th Annual New York Television Festival, at SVA Theatre, October 22, 2015 in New York City. | Matthew Eisman/WireImage Emmy-winning actress Catherine O'Hara (March 4, 1954-Jan. 30, 2026) was best-known for her roles on the sketch comedy series "SCTV," "Schitt's Creek," and the films "Home Alone" and "Beetlejuice." Born in Toronto, O'Hara grew up in a family that encouraged being funny, she told The New York Times in 2016: "My dad would tell jokes, and my mom would tell stories and imitate everyone within the stories. I think everyone is born with humor, but your life can beat it out of you, sadly, or you can be lucky enough to grow up in it." A member of the Second City improv troupe, where she originally understudied for Gilda Radner, O'Hara helped create the Canadian series "SCTV," for which she played a multitude of characters alongside cast members John Candy, Joe Flaherty, Eugene Levy, Andrea Martin, Dave Thomas and Harold Ramis. O'Hara dropped out of the cast for its third season, but rejoined after the show moved from syndication to NBC and then Cinemax. She won an Emmy as a co-writer. Among her movie roles, O'Hara played quirky supporting characters in Martin Scorsese's "After Hours" and Tim Burton's "Beetlejuice," and was also featured in "Dick Tracy," "The Paper," "Wyatt Earp," and "Orange County." But her most recognized role was as Macaulay Culkin's mother in "Home Alone." She was also part of Christopher Guest's ensemble in his improvisational mockumentaries, including "Waiting for Guffman," "Best in Show," "A Mighty Wind," and "For Your Consideration." Her biggest splash was as flamboyant matriarch Moira Rose in "Schitt's Creek." The show, created by her "SCTV" costar Eugene Levy and his son Dan, centers on a wealthy family losing all their money and being forced to live in a motel in a small town. In 2016 O'Hara told "CBS This Morning" she had some initial reservations about doing the series. "You never know how long it'd go, and to lock into one character, that's kind of scary," she said. "Schitt's Creek" ran for six years, and in its final season won nine Emmys. In addition to winning for playing Moira Rose in "Schitt's Creek," she was also Emmy-nominated for "Temple Grandin," "The Last of Us," and "The Studio." O'Hara shared with The New York Times her improv secret: "My crutch was, in improvs: when in doubt, play insane. Because you didn't have to excuse anything that came out of your mouth. It didn't have to make sense."

Dr. William Foege William Foege, physician and epidemiologist, receives the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama at the White House, May 29, 2012. | Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Dr. William Foege (March 12, 1936-Jan. 24, 2026), a physician and epidemiologist, was a leader in the global eradication of smallpox — one of humanity's greatest public health victories. His interest in global health was an outgrowth from his time when, at age 15, he was stuck in a body cast for three months. "We did not have television at that time," he said in a 2021 interview for Exemplars in Global Health. "So, I was forced to read, and came across Albert Schweitzer, and became interested in Africa, and in medicine." Following medical school, and years before he served as director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Foege was a member of the CDC's Epidemic Intelligence Service, as well as the Peace Corps, and studied at Harvard School of Public Health, where his interest in smallpox took hold. Smallpox vaccination campaigns were well established by that time. In fact, the disease was no longer seen in the U.S. But infections still occurred elsewhere. As a medical missionary in Nigeria in the 1960s, Foege and his colleagues developed a "ring containment" strategy, in which a smallpox outbreak was contained by identifying each smallpox case and vaccinating everyone with whom the patients might come into contact. The method relied heavily on quick detective work and was born out of necessity; there simply wasn't enough vaccine available to immunize everyone, Foege wrote in his 2011 book "House on Fire." It worked, and was instrumental in ending the spread of the disease. The last naturally-occurring case of smallpox was spotted in Somalia in 1977. Three years later, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated for good. From 1977 to 1983, Foege was director of the CDC. He was later executive director at The Carter Center, and senior fellow at the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. In 2012, he received the Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama. He was called "the Father of Global Health" by Duke University President Richard Brodhead. Foege said in the 2021 interview that he advises students to think about editing their own obituary every day: "'You won't realize it, but if you wake up in the morning knowing that you're going to edit your obituary, it makes a difference what you will try to do that day.' Is there a unifying field theory in all this? Yes. We belong to a group of optimists who believe that we can change the future. So, you wake up every morning knowing that you're changing the future."

"Uncle Floyd" Vivino "Uncle Floyd" (Floyd Vivino) photographed in New Jersey in 1984. | MPIRock/MediaPunch via Getty Images Beginning in the mid-1970s, "The Uncle Floyd Show" was a low-rent affair, broadcast from a UHF station whose studios were housed in an actual house in West Orange, New Jersey. Hosted by comedian and piano player Floyd Vivino (Oct. 19, 1951- Jan. 22, 2026), with a puppet named Oogie and a menagerie of vaudevillian sidekicks, the series — filled with corny jokes and skits, honky-tonk piano, musical acts, and letters from viewers — was ostensibly a children's variety show, but it played more as a parody of kids show hosts like Soupy Sales (and presaged later ironic kids shows like "Pee-Wee's Playhouse"). "We produced the shows without a script and never a rehearsal," he told NJ Arts in 2024. The show appealed to older kids and to punk artists (Cyndi Lauper, Bon Jovi and The Ramones were musical guests). When David Bowie met Vivino backstage at a New York appearance, he told him he'd learned of "The Uncle Floyd Show" from John Lennon. Bowie even name-checked Uncle Floyd in his song "Slip Away." "The Uncle Floyd Show" developed a cult following. A broadcast window on NBC's late-night schedule in the early '80s, airing after David Letterman, was short-lived, and the show returned to cable until 2001. Vivino, who hailed from a theatrical family and attended the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York, wore his love for all things New Jersey on his sleeve. (His anthem was "Deep in the Heart of Jersey.") In addition to his live revue shows and charity events, he hosted radio broadcasts and podcasts, and made a few film appearances, including playing an Armed Forces Radio DJ opposite Robin Williams in "Good Morning, Vietnam." In a 2011 newspaper interview, Vivino described giving a performance while a high school student in Glen Rock, N.J. in 1968: "The orchestra was playing 'Everything Is Coming Up Roses' and I felt the rush of 600 people clapping for me. It was then and there that I knew I was going to be an entertainer. I did not belong on the basketball court or in the science lab."

Valentino Valentino, pictured in Rome with his models in an undated photo. | Pascal CHEVALLIER/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images The designs of Valentino Garavani (May 11, 1932-Jan. 19, 2026) were fashion-show staples for nearly half a century. Known by his first name, Valentino clothed royals, first ladies and movie stars, from Jackie Kennedy Onassis, Princess Diana and Queen Rania of Jordan, to Julia Roberts and Cate Blanchett. Born into an affluent family in the northern Italian town of Voghera, his love of movies — and movie stars — lead him to fashion. He studied in Milan and Paris, and worked for designers Jean Desses and Guy Laroche, before launching his own firm in Rome in 1959. "Why I ever thought I could go out on my own like that, God only knows," Valentino told The New Yorker in 2005. "But my parents gave me a little money and I started. I had no idea what I was getting into. Sometimes ignorance is a wonderful thing." Besides his trademark shade of red, Valentino's recognized flourishes included bows, ruffles, lace and embroidery. Valentino's firm would expand to include ready-to-wear, menswear and accessories. In 1998, he and his partner, Giancarlo Giammetti, sold the label to an Italian holding company for an estimated $300 million, with Valentino remaining in a design role until 2008. In a 2016 interview with The Talks, Valentino said beauty was the most important thing to him: "Since I was a child I loved the way a dress looks, I admired a great face, a lovely body. I enjoy the beauty in a woman, in a man, in a child, in a painting. Beautiful things are important and make life important. Since I was a kid, I've been encouraging myself to appreciate beauty."

World.title: Netanyahu says "nobody had perfect foresight" on Iran's Strait of Hormuz blockade
World.content: Netanyahu says "nobody had perfect foresight" on Iran's Strait of Hormuz blockade CBS News chief Washington correspondent Major Garrett asked Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about The New York Times reporting that, in pre-war conversations with President Trump, Netanyahu and his team asserted that Iran would not choke off the Strait of Hormuz. CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes joins with Mr. Trump's response.

World.title: CDC leader says hantavirus not "a five-alarm fire bell"
World.content:
Washington — Jay Bhattacharya, the acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, defended the federal government's response to the deadly hantavirus outbreak, saying it doesn't make sense to sound "a five-alarm fire bell" because the risk to the public is "much, much lower" than what we saw with the COVID-19 pandemic.

"It's very different than COVID, and we should treat it differently than COVID," Bhattacharya told "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil on Monday when asked about the lack of daily briefings on the outbreak.

Bhattacharya, who also leads the National Institutes of Health, said hantavirus "is a more deadly disease if you get it," but added that the "epidemiological risk is very, very different" than COVID.

"Unlike COVID, the way that people get it from person to person is much, much more difficult for that to happen," he said of the way the virus spreads.

There have been at least three deaths and 10 confirmed or suspected cases of the rare, rodent-borne illness linked to the outbreak on the Dutch cruise ship MV Hondius, which had been sailing the Atlantic Ocean.

Eighteen American passengers who were aboard the ship returned to the U.S. on Monday and are being monitored at medical facilities in Nebraska and Georgia.

According to health officials, the hantavirus outbreak identified on the cruise ship is the Andes strain of the virus, which can spread between people but requires prolonged close contact with someone who is ill.

Bhattacharya said the U.S. has been tracking the outbreak for several weeks and is collaborating with state and local health departments, as well as the World Health Organization and foreign governments, on the response.

On communicating the potential danger to the public, Bhattacharya said the CDC does not want to cause unnecessary panic.

"The key thing is that we should be keeping the public aware of when there's actually threats to them, not causing the public to panic, not speculating about things that haven't happened, or potentially could in some universe happen," he said. "And being very, very clear about what we know and don't know, and also by responding appropriately when there is a risk, just as we've done."

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer criticized the Trump administration this week over last year's cuts to the CDC's Vessel Sanitation Program, which investigates outbreaks and conducts health inspections on cruise ships. Schumer, a Democrat from New York, called the decision "incompetence."

"The very CDC inspectors and port health workers we need to track this virus, the people whose entire job is to keep deadly diseases off cruise ships and out of our country, Donald Trump fired them. This White House will tell you the risk to Americans is low. How do they know? They have made it impossible to find out," Schumer said in a statement Sunday.

Bhattacharya told CBS News that in his two and half months in the role leading the CDC, he has seen "no gap at all in the group that manages outbreaks." Bhattacharya said the inspection team has done an "incredible job."

Bhattacharya also said the U.S. is prepared for any potential disease outbreaks during the upcoming World Cup, which is being jointly hosted by the U.S., Mexico and Canada in June and July.

"Of course, any time so many people are traveling, there's always the possibility of various outbreaks or whatnot to happen," he said. "But the risk is not any different than it is in other World Cups that we've managed properly. And the United States has systems in place to make sure that if something happens that we respond appropriately."

World.title: New poll finds a majority of Americans unsure if attempts on Trump's life were real
World.content:
New poll finds a majority of Americans unsure if attempts on Trump's life were real

toggle caption Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images

At a time of historically high political violence in the U.S., a substantial number of Americans doubt the legitimacy of recent attempts against President Trump's life.

Trump has been the subject of three assassination attempts over the last two years, however, a NewsGuard/YouGov poll released Monday finds that 30% of Americans think at least one of those incidents was staged.

The findings come just weeks after a gunman allegedly attempted to storm the White House Correspondents' Dinner, where Trump was in attendance, but was stopped at a security checkpoint by law enforcement before reaching the main ballroom. In the weeks since, a wave of misinformation around the event has spread online.

Sponsor Message

The poll surveyed 1,000 Americans between April 28 through May 4 and asked about the shooting at the correspondents' dinner, the assassination attempt against Trump in Butler, Penn. in July of 2024 and the attempt on his life that fall while golfing in West Palm Beach.

When given the options of "true," "false" or "not sure," and asked whether each of the incidents "was staged," a majority of respondents said they thought each event was either staged or said they were unsure. A plurality — roughly 45% — said each was a "real attempt."

One in four respondents believed the attempted attack at the correspondents' dinner was staged, according to the poll. The same was true for Butler, where 24% of respondents believed the attack was staged. Sixteen percent felt the same about the foiled plot in West Palm Beach.

Those views came despite numerous witnesses in Butler and Washington, D.C., and detailed federal indictments against the suspects in the Florida plot and the shooting at the dinner. A Senate committee investigated the attack in Butler after a Secret Service sniper killed the perpetrator, and put out an exhaustive report detailing security failures at the rally.

Sofia Rubinson is a senior editor at NewsGuard, which tracks false claims that spread online. Claims posted on X within the week after the dinner garnered over 90 million views, she said.

Sponsor Message

"There's really not a lot of evidence that these social media users are citing or relying on," she said. "It's really just this belief and this distrust that the government is acting honestly and is giving us accurate information."

During an interview with 60 Minutes the day after the dinner, Trump dismissed claims that the incident was staged.

"I think they're more sick than they are con people," Trump said, alluding to individuals pushing such conspiracy theories. "But there's a lot of con in there too."

The new poll finds that doubts about the assassination attempts are far more concentrated among younger Americans and Democrats.

According to the poll, Americans 18-29 were the most likely of any generation to believe all three events were staged.

It's a sentiment also more pronounced on the left, with 21% of Democrats feeling that way, seven times more than Republicans. When asked about all three incidents, larger shares of Democrats say each event was staged, with 34% saying that about the correspondents' dinner, 42% about Butler and 26% about Trump's golf club.

Though Republicans were less likely to think the events were fabricated, Rubinson notes a striking increase in the number of GOP voters who think the shooting at the dinner was staged — 13% — compared to the events at Butler (7%) and Trump's golf club (7%.)

"Still [a] much smaller percentage than Democrats. But we're seeing that Republicans are increasingly more likely to believe this, 'staged,' narrative," she said.

Rubinson acknowledged that while it's difficult to definitively explain that increase, it could be because of a "splintering" within Trump's movement over issues like the administration's handling of the Epstein files as well as the war with Iran.

"A lot of the traditional MAGA base is … maybe growing increasingly discontent with the Trump administration and more prone to believing these types of conspiracies."

World.title: Abortion pill by mail allowed for at least 3 more days, the Supreme Court says
World.content:
Abortion pill by mail allowed for at least 3 more days, the Supreme Court says

toggle caption Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

The Supreme Court on Monday gave itself more time to consider a national ban on telemedicine access to the abortion pill mifepristone.

Justice Samuel Alito extended an earlier order he issued by three more days, so rules for prescribing mifepristone online or through the mail remain in effect through Thursday at a minimum.

The case at issue

The tumult over the future of telemedicine access to mifipristone started on May 1 with a ruling from the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals. That ruling re-instituted prescribing rules from before the pandemic that required patients to receive mifepristone in person in a doctor's office or clinic.

Sponsor Message

The Food and Drug Administration determined that the rule was medically unnecessary in 2021. The state of Louisiana sued last fall, arguing that telemedicine access undermines the state's abortion ban.

What is telemedicine abortion?

The telemedicine abortion process starts with a patient connecting with a healthcare provider on the phone or online. If the patient is eligible, that provider can prescribe two medications — mifepristone and another pill called misoprostol. Patients can pick up the medicine at a local pharmacy, or providers can mail the drugs to a patient's home.

That access is a big part of the reason why the number of abortions nationally has actually increased since the Supreme Court overturned the constitutional right to abortion in 2022. Now, most abortions in the U.S. use this combination of medications, and one quarter happen via telemedicine.

After the 5th Circuit ruling, some providers said they would continue offering telemedicine access to abortion medication using a different protocol that involves higher doses of misoprostol and no mifepristone.

Researchers say that method is just as safe and effective, but tends to cause more pain for patients and more side effects, like nausea and diarrhea. Misoprostol has other medical uses, such as treating gastric ulcers and hemorrhage, and has been on the market longer than mifepristone. It is likely to remain fully accessible, even if mifepristone is restricted.

Sponsor Message

Since the FDA's prescribing rules for medications apply to the whole country, a change to the rules about how mifepristone can be accessed has national impact. That means it affects states with constitutionally-protected access to abortion, states with criminal bans, like Louisiana, and all states in between.

States' rights
